Handicapped Scuba Divers

By: Efpe Senekal | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Scuba diving, exchanging a wheelchair for a wetsuit, the Handicapped Scuba Association trains the severely disabled to enjoy the freedom of an underwater environment.

Summary:
A dive-a-thon, organised by the Handicapped Scuba Association, focuses the attention on a very special group of free spirits, confined in severely disabled bodies. Melissa Leonard has been confined to a wheelcahir since the age of six. For years she had a dream of being able to scuba dive but she had no idea where or how to go about it. Five years ago she was introduced to an instructor who specialises in teaching handicapped scuba divers. This turned out to be a life changing event for Melissa, learning to be safe in the potentially hazardous underwater environment took a lot of hard work and many hours in the pool. Divers have to be able to retrieve a regulator and clear a mask, amongst other skills. These actions require free movement of the hands and arms, even a simple movement like holding one's nose to equalize pressure in the ears, is impossible for some disabled divers. Scuba divers always dive in buddy pairs. Handicapped scuba divers require specially trained dive buddies to look after them throughout the dive, keeping them upright and constantly communicating with them. Braam Le Roux is a PADI diving instructor that specialises in training handicapped divers. We will look at his motivation for doing this very demanding type of training. Melisssa has found a whole new circle of friends through her diving activities and we will meet some of them and get to know their stories, Francois is a blind diver, he lost his sight 6 years ago in an accident, Cherise became a quadroplegic after a motor vehicle accident in 2014, at the age of 22, her scuba experience forms part of her re-hab. Vic Hugo suffered brain damage and use of his right hand side, he's the "official videographer" and a live wire in the handicapped scuba diving community, we will get to know him better. We will meet the dive buddies and instructors and film them under water with our characters.

Press Release:


Disabled Divers
It’s one of the most dangerous things a disabled person can attempt. Yet, with skilled dive buddies on hand to perform every function from moving a disabled person through the water to equalising their ears and monitoring every vital process, physically disabled people can enjoy the freedom of underwater weightlessness. Carte Blanche takes a camera into the deep to meet the courageous people who exchange their wheelchairs for wet suits.


Script:


Handicapped scuba divers- transcript


Bongani Voice over:
The self contained under water breathing apparatus, better known as scuba, was invented in 1943 by Jaques Cousteau and Emile Gagnan.
Scuba diving has enabled millions of divers to explore the depths of the oceans in relative safety and comfort.
Far away from the ocean, near the North West town of Brits, is a disused chromium mine. When mining operations hit an underground water source, the opencast mine was flooded by spring water. Miracle Waters is now a popular inland scuba diving site where many divers learn how to dive in open water.

Bongani on camera:
As an adventure sport, scuba diving requires dedication and training. But what's particularly special about what's happening here, is that anybody can do it.

Voice Over:
Dougie Coetzee is a scuba diver, he is also a quadroplegic after he broke his neck seventeen years ago.

Bongani on camera:
What's it like for you to have been able to do this?

Dougie on camera:
Well, brilliant hey, ja it's awesome, it's a whole different world down there.... and ah, it's a bit of freedom as well for a guy that's stuck in a wheelchair the whole time.

Voice Over:
Dougie is here as part of the Handicapped Scuba Association of South Africa's fifty hour dive-a-thon. Better known as HSA, the Handicapped Scuba Association trains divers with various disabilities to scuba dive and enjoy the freedom to be found in the aquatic environment. Braam Le Roux is a PADI dive instructor that specialises in training Handicapped scuba divers.

Interview with Braam on jetty:
Bongani:
Tell me about this weekend, what are you doing here?
Braam le Roux:
This weekend we do the dive-a-thon, where we dive 50 hours non stop, from Friday ten-o-clock till Sunday one-o-clock, to raise money to put some funds in HSA's account, the non profit, and also to train new people coming in.

Melissa was first diagnosed with muscular dystrophy, a degenerative muscle disease, at the age of sixteen months. She's been permanently confined to a wheelchair since eight. She's now a director of the Handicapped Scuba Association of South Africa.

Interview Bongani Melissa office:
Bongani:
Melissa, when did your journey with disability begin?
Melissa Leonard:
When I started to walk, I looked like a normal child and at the age of sixteen months I started to fall and my parents noticed it and took me to the doctors and the doctors diagnosed me with muscular dystrophy.
Bogani:
And how did that diagnosis change your life?
Melissa:
W hen I got the wheelchair for the first time it was hard accepting it, I was about eight and it was difficult for me but it aided me in my school journey.

Bogani:
Do you remember walking?
Melissa:
I can't really... I just remember having difficulty walking but I can't remember the feeling of walking, so ja..

Since Melissa took up scuba diving in 2011, she has become very proficient in the water

Bongani on camera:
Tell me about the feeling of being almost weightless under water.
Melissa:
Oh, it's awesome, like you can actually move yourself, your legs and whatever, without feeling the gravity. So, you're light under water.
Bongani:
What challenges do you face when you're scuba diving?
Melissa:
Ok, well, I'm not able to dive by myself. I need my dive buddy to physically hold me the whole time under water so my buddy steers me wherever we go and physically holds mein the same position. Or else I'm going to be like an astronaut, going alll over the place.

Bongani to Dougie on jetty:
So, when you tell people that you go diving, do they get surprised?
Dougie:
I'm supposed to be paralysed from my neck down. As a guy that can barely do anything for himself, it's nice under water if you can, you know, kind of move by yourself, swim by yourself.
Bongani
So how many dive have you done?
Dougie:
I've done about seven dives or here at Miracle Waters, just to do all the courses, and then I've been down to the coast twice now, so, I mean the ocean is a different world, a different environment, it's like being in a fish tank.

Bongani Voice Over:
Dougie works as an IT manager for a large financial concern. We visited him shortly after he'd returned from a diving trip to Mozambique.

Bongani in Dougie's house:
Doug, how did you become disabled?
Dougie:
I walked through a waterfall, about seventeen years ago. I went fishing with a couple of my friends, I saw a waterfall on the side and decided to see what's at the back, didn't find anything there and then I thought on my way back: "This water can't be that strong, and I was going to walk straight through it", you know, like the main stream in front of me. And I just, I just opened my arms like this and I just walked, and the force just threw me down between the rocks. And I broke my neck. Straight afterwards, I woke up lying down in the river. Now I'd just broken my neck and I can't turn myself around, I can't breathe, so, I also drowned, straight afterwards. And my friends were all still behind the waterfall, so they didn't see me. So, after a couple of minutes, they eventually came out and they saw me drifting there. When they turned me around, I was blue already, one of them gave me mouth to mouth and they brought me back.

Bongani Voice Over:

Scuba diving, like most sports, has its challenges. Proper training is essential for safe diving and the instructors take on a huge responsibility when they train handicapped divers. Patrick Voorma is the regional manager for the Professional Association of Diving instructors.

Patrick Voorma:
From a training organisation point of view, we don't give these guys any leeway, they have to master the skill as an able bodied person. What we now expect from the instructor, is that the instructor adapts his teaching techniques, and adapts the way of doing the skill, that the student can then master the performance requirement and actually master that skill. We put a lot of pressure on the instructor to find ways for the student to meet that skill.

Bongani to Braam on jetty:
What made you want to instruct disabled people?
Braam:
Ja, it's a calling for me, to help these people to scuba dive. The rehab for these people is just unbelievable. I saw people really changing, just on the first day they start scuba diving. I really see changing in them, their personalities, the rehabs and all that kind of thing.

Bongani Voice Over:
Divers have to be able to retrieve a regulator and clear a mask, amongst other skills. These actions require free movement of the hands and arms, even a simple movement like holding one's nose to equalize pressure in the ears, is impossible for some disabled divers.

Braam:
The quadroplegics, we actually function for them and we equalise the whole time for them until we're going down there and then we finish it.

Dougie:
Well, actually, it's only of late I've learned how to equalise and you know, trying to push and close my nose, move my mouth around and doing the equalising thing. But in the beginning it was tricky, ja, so we had buddies to close my nose for me, to equalise.

Braam:
So there's certain things we train the guys, our instructors, uhm, it's like quadroplegics, if you take them down, we can't tilt them because they can't cough, by themselves. They mustn't get water in theirs masks, so there's certain ways of taking them down, at a 45 angle until you're down, and from there we go on.

Bongani Voice Over:
Francois Neethling is a blind diver who lost his sight fifteen years ago due to a genetic condition.

Bongani:
How did you get involved in scuba diving?

Francois Neethling:
As a blind or visually impaired diver, scuba diving is not actually a sport for blind bacause you have to see the corals, the fish and that's what it's actually about.
For me opened a different world again, I never knew that there was disabled people out there, until it happened with me. I had a big shock and "wow, ok, now what? Am I gonna live?" And I think, after that, getting to meet people with disabilities, understanding what is the life out there, and their capabilities, a completely new life has opnede up for me, completely new life. And that has brought a new perspective of respect for people, respect for what is out there, and what a person can or cannot do.
But it's for me to go down and have the silence, own time for that moment and that freedom. That's what it's given me.

Melissa:
It's opened so many doors for me, I got to meet new people, I got to go places and I get to do things with friends you know. Many doors opened because before I started scuba diving I was like, at home, not really getting the opportunities to go out. But once I started scuba diving, I got the opportunity to go to Mozambique, accross the border for the first time, it was really awesome, it was like an adventure.

Bongani on camera:
This is a painting of the disabled divers going on their first trip to the sea, and it speaks to the kind of support they receive.

Bongani Voice Over:
This is a painting of the disabled divers going on their first trip to the sea, and it speaks of the kind of support they receive. Divers from all over South Africa contributed and took part in the successful dive-a-thon, that went a long way towards helping some of the handicapped divers realise their dreams of diving in the ocean.

Patrick Voorma:
As an extreme scuba diver, you tend to forget that you got into it for the everyday fun part of scuba diving. When the guys approached me from HSA to get involved, I jumped at the opportunity because I actually wanted to go and experience something I experienced before, and actually dive with people with physical challenges. And for me it was a, it was actually a sort of a .life changing experience, because here were people taht had their own challenges and were doing the extreme extent of what they could do, and they were doing it quite comfortably in the water. It sort of hit home to me how amazing scuba diving is a sport, it's that we can all do it and we can all do it at the same levels, no matter what your cahllenges are above the water.
